extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, patent policy makers, and patent quality researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and metrics for evaluating patent examination quality, focusing on examiner prior-art search proficiency, handling of prior-art rejections, interview practice, claim interpretation, continuity treatment, and patent/exam characteristics correlated with litigation and IPR risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's prior art search proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reviewers' opinion, the examiner’s search was deficient in more than half (37 prosecution histories or 61 percent) of the cases for which the PTAB determined that at least one claim was unpatentable over prior art not found by the examiner’s search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: the sample is self-selected (IPR-petitioned patents), reviewers may be subject to hindsight or confirmation bias, and reviewers did not perform independent prior-art searches. Recommendation: expand the study with reviewer-blind reviews and have reviewers conduct their own prior art searches as in general compliance review to better assess adequacy of examiner searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons a search is considered deficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated reasons (Figure 6-5) why an examiner’s search may be deemed deficient: 'Search is too limiting', 'Required class/subclass not included', 'Poor use of proximity and Boolean operators', 'No inventor's name search', and 'Other reason'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that the choice 'search is too limiting' can encompass many different search defects (failure to consult appropriate databases; failure to employ appropriate search terms, including technical terms, controlled vocabulary, and inventor information; failure to use truncation, proximity, and Boolean operators; failure to review relevant sections of the patent classification system). A more focused questionnaire would allow more meaningful conclusions about specific search defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure access to and use of STIC and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable examiners to do the best job possible of finding prior art by ensuring STIC (Scientific and Technical Information Center) can continue to offer up-to-date services, and that examiners are aware of and can fully utilize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and expand examiner participation in training opportunities offered by database providers. Use pre-issuance third-party submissions, crowdsourcing, and other innovative means to ensure the best prior art is available early in examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's handling of prior art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When examiners rely on a reference as the basis of a prior art rejection, they most often do so properly; examiners usually make appropriate decisions regarding withdrawal of rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data: out of 78 IPR proceedings, only four (5%) had a claim found unpatentable by PTAB based on a prior-art rejection previously made by the examiner but later withdrawn. Examiners generally do not limit a reference to anticipation-only when it could support obviousness. These findings suggest competent application of recognized references once examiners identify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent reasons for examiner withdrawal of rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner withdraws a rejection, apparent reasons include: claim interpretation, consideration of applicant's arguments, consideration of interview held, and other reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 6-6 breaks down counts of rejections and apparent reasons. Monitoring these reasons can identify procedural or substantive areas for improvement in prosecution practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper treatment of application continuity claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should properly treat continuity claims including domestic benefit claims, foreign priority claims, and U.S. national stage entries under 35 U.S.C. § 371.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data: Of 78 cases, 50 included a domestic benefit claim, 9 included foreign priority, and 5 were § 371 national stage; a continuity claim was mishandled by the examiner in only one domestic benefit situation, suggesting continuity handling errors are not a significant driver of IPR filings in this sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordation of substantive interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular patent prosecution procedure requires the examiner to ensure that a written record of any substantive interview be included in the prosecution history. The written record need not be separately indexed in PALM; it may be part of another Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers were asked to count interviews separately indexed and those not. Of 78 cases, at least one interview formed part of the prosecution history in 27 cases (35%). Low interview rates could indicate value of interviews; further study with larger sample advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of interview summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The interview record should provide either a clear and complete summary of the interview or a statement of agreement with a summary provided by the attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 6-5: Of 42 total interviews, 28 (66.7%) were assessed as having either a clear and complete summary or agreement with the attorney's summary. Proper summary promotes clear prosecution history and reduces disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview outcomes as quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews should be assessed by whether they: resulted in an examiner amendment; indicated allowable subject matter; provided correct suggestions to overcome rejections; and whether the applicant adopted examiner suggestions resulting in allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 6-5 provides reviewer assessments (percentages) for these outcomes. These items serve as measurable indicators of the substantive effectiveness of interviews in advancing prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation consistency and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare examiner and PTAB claim interpretations; disagreements may affect patentability. In the study, examiner and PTAB disagreed in 18% (14 cases) and the difference impacted patentability in 9 cases (12% of total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiatives like the Glossary Pilot Program (launched to promote claim clarity) may reduce disagreements about claim construction by encouraging clear explanations of claim terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding reviewer selection and hindsight biases in assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating examiner performance in cases that were petitioned for IPR, account for self-selection and potential reviewer hindsight/confirmation bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because petitioned patents are not representative, reviewers should, where possible, be blind to IPR status and conduct independent prior-art searches. Normal OPQA compliance reviews (which show 90-95% of reviewers do not uncover better prior art than examiners) provide context suggesting caution in generalizing results from IPR-selected samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-examination variables most predictive of litigation/IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables outside direct control of the USPTO — entity size, foreign origin, and number of domestic parent applications — were the most important in predicting likelihood of subsequent litigation and IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models using only these variables perform almost as well as full models. Office policy (e.g., small-entity fees) can indirectly affect these variables by shaping which entities seek patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of independent claims as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents with more independent claims are more likely to be involved in subsequent litigation and IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider this as a characteristic correlated with downstream challenges; further research needed to parse causation vs correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words per independent claim (claim breadth/clarity) as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents with fewer words per independent claim are more likely to be involved in subsequent litigation and IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may reflect narrower, less detailed claim drafting or technology lexicon issues; more study is needed to determine whether this arises from examination quality or inherent invention characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: GS-level of the allowing examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: The GS-level of the allowing examiner is correlated with litigation/IPR outcomes: patents allowed by lower GS-level examiners are generally less likely to be asserted or petitioned for IPR; GS-level was also the most significant variable in comparing instituted vs. non-instituted IPR-petitioned patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity remains (e.g., GS-13 examiners in Signatory Review Program may allow only clear/narrow claims). Interpretation requires caution and further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of IDS filings as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of Information Disclosure Statements (IDS) filed tends to be positively associated with a greater chance of litigation and IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may signal applicant belief in higher patent value and thus correlate with downstream challenges; consider whether citation of large numbers of references impedes examiners' ability to locate the most relevant references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of examiner interviews as predictor
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of interviews is positively associated with litigation (may signal higher patent value or more contested prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews may be more frequent for applications believed to be more valuable; interpret association carefully as a potential value signal rather than a causal effect of interviews on disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance without previous rejection (first-action allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents allowed on first action are correlated with litigation outcomes: allowed-on-first-action patents are likely to contain clearer and more narrowly drafted claims, which may reduce challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variable had measurable but smaller impact than non-examination variables; consider claim clarity as a mediating factor in downstream dispute risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor PTAB decisions and changing legal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between examiner and PTAB outcomes may reflect changes in law (e.g., KSR, Bilski, Myriad, Mayo) and USPTO guidance; track whether unpatentability decisions are due to examination error or changes in standards between grant and petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue research and monitoring as IPR proceedings mature and law/practice evolve to identify whether trends persist and to guide initiatives for enhancing patent quality.
